document.title: Post-Technical Conference Comments of PPL Electric Utilities Corporation re PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms
document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder 
Reforms 
Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
POST-TECHNICAL CONFERENCE COMMENTS  
OF PPL ELECTRIC UTILITIES CORPORATION 
 
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) held a technical 
conference July 23, 2026, to discuss PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) governance and stake-
holder processes, focusing on potential reforms to improve PJM’s ability to address operational 
and market needs in a timely and efficient manner.1 It now invites post-conference comments re-
lated to issues raised that interested persons believe would benefit from further discussion.2 
FERC also includes an Appendix listing 20 yes/no questions focused on the themes, concerns, 
and potential points of consensus that emerged during the conference.3 PPL Electric Utilities 
Corporation (PPL Electric) thanks the Commission for raising these important questions and re-
sponds as follows: 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
 
As Chairman Swett said at the onset of the technical conference, “We need change. The 
market is facing change, and we’re not going to succeed without it.”4 Deputy Secretary Danly 
 
1 See PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms, Notice of Commission-Led Technical Conference, 
Docket No. AD26-7 (May 12, 2026).  
2 See PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms, Notice Requesting Post-Conference Comment, Docket 
No. AD26-7 (Jul. 30, 2026) (“Post-Conference Notice”).  
3 Id. at 3–6.  
4 Swett, Tr. at 11:7–16.

2 
 
highlighted the need for change, saying “PJM is a mess … [with] two auctions in a row that 
failed to meet the capacity requirement. That is not a functioning market.”5 Several panelists fo-
cused on potential changes to governance authority and decision-making roles.  Deputy Secre-
tary Danly, however, framed the core issue more directly:  “Who is responsible for what?”6 and 
the “number one priority” being the resource adequacy crisis (how can we “get[] as much supply 
online as quickly as possible … while protecting ratepayers”7). Deputy Secretary Danly also 
highlighted the filing rights issue: saying “we are deviating from the basic premise of the Federal 
Power Act and, indeed, basically every state commission law, which is you have a utility that 
files its tariff revisions.”8  
 
Following the technical conference, the region is now discussing deep changes to PJM’s 
structure, governing documents, and decision-making processes. Proposals include changes to 
both Board function and makeup, changes to the stakeholder process and Member control, 
changes to the interaction between the states and the Regional Transmission Organization 
(RTO), and reallocation of federal filing rights. In response, PPL Electric reiterates many of the 
points it made in its Pre-Technical Conference Comments: (1) The PJM Board must be empow-
ered with full control over all substantive roles of PJM delegated to PJM by the PJM Transmis-
sion Owners.9 This includes moving the Planning Protocol and other substantive language out of 
the Operating Agreement where it is purportedly under Member control, in tension with the 
 
5 Danly, Tr. at 32:23–33:18.  
6 Danly, Tr. at 34:2–25 (recognizing that a public utility with a responsible Board operating under the 
oversight of a public utility commission is a model that works; RTOs have a “different model” where “it’s 
unclear exactly who it is that’s responsible for what”).  
7 Danly, Tr. at 38:21–39:3.  
8 Danly, Tr. at 36:8–21.  
9 PPL Electric Pre-Technical Conference Comments at 5.

3 
 
Federal Power Act. (2) FERC has limited authority over internal governance of the RTOs, but it 
should encourage PJM to pursue changes that empower the Board and increase its independ-
ence.10 These changes may include longer terms for Board members, reducing restrictions on 
Member-affiliated individuals serving or shortening the “cooling off” period, and allowing more 
communication between Board members and Stakeholders. (3) The stakeholder process should 
be changed from a governance role to an advisory role.11 Other changes to the stakeholder pro-
cess, like reducing the number of sectors or changing the voting rules would then be less im-
portant but may still be valuable. Finally, (4) The states must increase their role at PJM, espe-
cially if the deregulated states change their energy policies to address resource adequacy and del-
egate some of their authority in that realm to PJM.12 Although PPL Electric remains open to dis-
cussions of formal state governance roles or changes to filing rights, the Commission should be 
aware these are likely to create significant litigation risk and delay that will distract from the co-
ordination necessary to address Deputy Secretary Danly’s “number one priority.”13  PPL Electric 
also notes that many PJM Transmission Owners support several of these core reforms, including 
moving toward a more advisory stakeholder process and providing PJM with section 205 filing 
rights over core RTO functions such as the energy and ancillary service markets and the RTEP 
process.  At the same time, stakeholders have expressed differing views regarding proposals to 
grant states or stakeholder bodies alternative filing rights or other formal roles in the section 205 
process.  PPL Electric submits these comments separately to address those issues and the legal 
and policy considerations they present.   
 
10 Id. at 6.  
11 Id. at 7, 11.  
12 Id. at 8.  
13 See Note 7, supra.

4 
 
II. 
COMMENTS 
A. 
Board Makeup, Selection, and Independence  
 
Many commentators across the spectrum support changes to the PJM Board makeup and 
selection process. One relatively straightforward change is extending the term of individual 
Board members. This was proposed or supported by Mr. Finkel,14 Mr. Mills,15 and Ms. Philips,16 
among others. PPL Electric agrees with extending the Board term.17 Relatedly, there was some 
discussion of a preference for Board members who live in the region.18 This, however, must be 
tied to loosening of rules restricting potential Board members from serving because of business 
connections to PJM Members. In other words, knowledgeable, qualified people dedicated to the 
success of PJM and the PJM markets are exactly the people who are excluded by the current con-
flicts rules.19 One option for resolving this would be to move from a two-year stay out to a one-
year stay out.20 PPL Electric supports this commonsense change, and would add a slight prefer-
ence for Board candidates with some geographic connection to the region, so long as it does not 
impact candidate quality.21 
 
14 Finkel, Tr. at 77:10–12 (“I think we all agree on longer board terms”). 
15 Mills, Tr. at 70:4–16; 71:1–16; 72:22–73:6 (preference for “six to nine years” for a term).  
16 Philips, Tr. at 72:4–15 (“Maybe five years sounds very reasonable”).  
17 See PPL Electric Pre-Technical Conference Comments at 6.  
18 See Commissioner See, Tr. at 20:13–18 (getting "more members in the PJM region … with direct expe-
rience" is low-hanging fruit); Commissioner Rosner, Tr. at 224:18–21 ("some amount of the board lives 
in the region, to get that better understanding and more engagement with the states"); Moskowitz, Tr. at 
255:4–8 (“there probably should be requirements, to tie more board members – to make sure that they 
have connections to the PJM region”).  
19 See Thomas, Tr. at 225:9–21 (“it is challenging finding qualified candidates that pass all the screens in 
terms of conflicts …”); Bruce, Tr. at 249:4–13; 250:4–7 (“people that have expertise in the energy space, 
they touch in some respects PJM. So, that limits the pool.”).  
20 Bruce, Tr. at 250:17–251:10.  
21 See PPL Pre-Technical Conference Comments at 6.

5 
 
 
 More contentious is the question of who selects the Board. Some state representatives 
have proposed  a significant voting role for state representatives on the PJM Nominating Com-
mittee, including a proposal for three voting seats.22  Mr. Finkel defended that proposal at the 
technical conference as  designed to achieve “rough parity” with other interests represented on 
the Committee.23 Others supported some form of state representation in the nomination process, 
although not necessarily the same structure, number of seats, or level of voting authority.24 Left 
unsaid at the technical conference is the fact that roughly half of the existing PJM Members al-
ready represent customers or customer-aligned interests (including state actors like consumer ad-
vocates voting in the End Use Customer sector and municipal entities voting in the Electric Dis-
tribution Sector) rather than “private interests.” This means that companies investing billions of 
dollars in PJM would be left with at most three, and more likely two (Generation Owners and 
Transmission Owners), of ten seats—a materially reduced role in contested votes. This is not a 
recipe for an independent Board, nor one likely to establish market rules that invite the signifi-
cant investment in the transmission and generation systems necessary to solve the resource ade-
quacy crisis.  
 
But setting aside whether it is a good idea for the states to control the energy markets via 
a working majority on the Nominating Committee, FERC has no authority to order this change. 
As laid out in PPL Electric’s pre-technical conference comments, FERC cannot dictate the 
 
22 PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms, Pre-Technical Conference Statement of Jacob Finkel, Of-
fice of Governor Josh Shapiro, on behalf of the PJM Governors’ Collaborative, Docket No. AD26-7-000 
(Jul. 16, 2026) (“Finkel Pre-Technical Conference Statement”) at 9. 
23 See Finkel, Tr. at 101:13–102:1. This controlling stake is even deeper if the individual Nominating 
Committee members can veto a proposed Board member absent their unanimous support.  
24 See Bagot, Tr. at 109:20–110:4 (“it makes sense for the governors to play a role on the nominating 
committee”); Commissioner See, Tr. at 21:5–10 (“State representation on the nominating committee 
seems an obvious step forward”).

6 
 
internal governance mechanisms of entities under its regulatory oversight.25 A Commission order 
giving the states control over the Nominating Committee would fly in the face of the holding in 
the CAISO case and invite almost certain and immediate litigation.26 Regardless of the strength 
or prominence of the proposals, or the number and fervor/salience of the voices raising them, 
Congress has simply not delegated FERC the power to force this change.  
 
Luckily there are compromises available that will accomplish many of the same goals 
without opening the litigation floodgates or introducing massive uncertainty into the PJM mar-
kets. There was extensive support at the technical conference for increased coordination between 
the Board and the states, and limited opposition to more reasonable proposals such as a state rep-
resentative (OPSI or the governors) participating in the Nominating Committee as a non-voting 
member.27 This can, at minimum, be considered a reasonable first step to help deepen the com-
munication and coordination paths between the states and PJM while deeper changes are held for 
a (hopefully) less volatile future. PPL Electric supports such a compromise.  
B. 
Stakeholder Process Changes 
 
Significant time at the technical conference was devoted to the stakeholder process itself. 
Concerns focused on a variety of issues, including failure to move issues forward,28 voting 
 
25 See PPL Electric Pre-Technical Conference Comments at 6 (FERC has a limited role in “how the Board 
is selected and how it exercises power”).  
26 See California Independent System Operator Corp. v. FERC, 372 F. 3d 395, 403 (2004). 
27 This is similar to the ISO-NE proposal as described by Ms. Gulluni. See Tr. at 79:8–80:8 (proposing a 
non-voting OPSI member “to get confidence in the integrity of the process” but also recognizing issues 
with state participation including confidentiality, FOIA, and politization).  
28 Danly, Tr. at 37:18–22 (“issue charges that are critical cannot make it over the threshold even to be 
considered”).

7 
 
transparency,29 the relevance of lower-level committees,30 meeting cadence,31 and voting rules.32 
The most important proposed change though, and one that PPL Electric wholeheartedly en-
dorses, is a move to advisory voting.33 Making the stakeholders advisory to the Board would dra-
matically reduce fights over procedure and voting rules, because filings over the Board’s objec-
tion (or Member vetoes of Board actions) would be off the table. Instead, stakeholder discussions 
would be reframed into an effort to provide the best answer to the Board.34  
 
Making the stakeholder process advisory on substantive matters is a relatively easy fix. 
Stakeholders are already advisory over most of the PJM Tariff, other governing documents, and 
Manuals.35 All that would be formally required is moving the substantive schedules (Schedules 
1, 2, 6, 6a, and 6b) from the Operating Agreement to the Tariff36 and some corresponding 
changes to other governing documents, including to the CTOA.37 Although the discussion at the 
technical conference focused on whether this could be compelled due to Mobile-Sierra 
 
29 Commissioner LeCerte, Tr. at 28:21–24 (“PJM has a binding stakeholder process that is untransparent 
and designed to protect the interests of those who profit”).  
30 Haque, Tr. at 145:18–22 (questioning lower committee relevance); but see Lieberman, Tr. at 147:12–
148:5 (defending them as focusing “subject matter experts on a specific issue”).  
31 Lieberman, Tr. at 148:8–149:7.  
32 E.g., Quinn, Tr. at 156:24–158:8 (agreeing to conform lower-level affiliate voting with senior commit-
tee sector-weighted voting).  
33 Lake, Tr. at 48:24–49:4; see also id. at 50:21–22 (“They need a voice in the stakeholder process but it 
cannot be a veto”); Burbure, Tr. at 57:8–13 (“stakeholders should have a voice but not a veto”).  
34 Jaworski, Tr. at 170:10–172:13 (arguing stakeholders can provide expertise and states can provide stra-
tegic direction); Quinlan, Tr. at 151:12–153:2 (“there’s really no replacement for the breadth of the PJM 
stakeholders and their expertise”); Anders, Tr. at 245:5–11 (even in an advisory role, there is “tremendous 
value in the stakeholder processes”).  
35 Quinn, Tr. at 179:2–21 (recognizing the capacity market, the reason behind the resource adequacy crisis 
and the focus on PJM, is already under the PJM Board’s control and subject to an advisory stakeholder 
process); but see PPL Electric Pre-Technical Conference Comments at 20 (highlighting PJM practice of 
following stakeholder direction even where not strictly required).  
36 PPL Electric Pre-Technical Conference Comments at 7, 16–18; Haque, Tr. at 196:22–197:24.  
37 PPL Electric Pre-Technical Conference Comments at 17–18; Chandler, Tr. at 198:4–199:25.

8 
 
protections, the fact is that the PJM Transmission Owners largely (if not unanimously) support 
the proposed movement of these schedules and stand ready to help facilitate. Indeed, as high-
lighted in the technical conference discussion, it was the other sectors of the Members Commit-
tee who opposed giving control of the planning protocol to the PJM Board.38 
C. 
Section 205 Rights and “Jump Ball” Proposals 
 
Another major topic at the technical conference was the allocation of Federal Power Act 
section 20539 filing rights among PJM, the PJM Transmission Owners, the PJM Members, and 
potentially the states or other parties. As discussed above, the clearest and most straightforward 
change would be to give PJM “205 rights over all of its core business functions.”40 Mr. Mills, 
speaking for the Board, was clear: “We believe that the Board would be more independent and 
able to act more quickly if [it] had those 205 rights over the Operating Agreement, which is the 
energy and ancillary services market.”41 Such a change would require either member support, or 
more likely a section 206 complaint against the Operating Agreement.42 Unlike the more esoteric 
governance change proposals discussed throughout the technical conference, this change is 
 
38 Moskowitz, Tr. at 236:12–237:1; see also PPL Electric Pre-Technical Conference Comments at 17 and 
Note 33 (citing PJM Members Committee vote against moving Planning Protocol to Tariff despite over-
whelming transmission owner support). Notably, this vote did not include the more controversial lan-
guage in the CTOA that led the formal opposition to the transmission owner / PJM amendments to that 
agreement.  
39 FPA Section 205, 16 U.S.C. § 824d (governing how public utilities establish and change rates through 
Commission filings).   
40 Haque, Tr. at 197:4–24.  
41 Mills, Tr. at 68:9–69:16.  
42 See Anders, Tr. at 231:1–234:5 (doubting member support for giving PJM filing authority over the sub-
stantive schedules to the Operating Agreement and suggesting FERC could order a change under § 206).

9 
 
directly tied to FERC’s authority over substantive transmission and markets provisions, and 
many stakeholders (including transmission owners) are committed to supporting the effort.43 
 
The second large, and more controversial, proposed change to filing rights was the pro-
posal to give the states a “jump ball” or other form of filing rights, either over resource adequacy 
or more broadly. Again, Mr. Finkel’s proposal was the strongest assertion of state power, arguing 
that “[f]or matters of shared responsibility, PJM should agree to file an alternative state proposal 
when the RTO intends to submit a 205 filing.”44 This is not a claim of filing rights for the states 
per se, which would be illegal under the Federal Power Act, but is still widely understood to be 
of questionable legality.45 PPL Electric’s position remains that, while states have a central role to 
play in generation planning and resource adequacy—one that requires their deep coordination 
with PJM—they cannot be assigned or exercise section 205 filing rights unless consistent with 
the Federal Power Act and applicable precedent.46  
 
However, PPL Electric remains open to further discussion of how the states can exert 
some control over PJM in one specific scenario: If, as is necessary to address the resource ade-
quacy crisis, the deregulated states significantly reform their generation planning and other en-
ergy policies, and in so doing delegate powers of their own to PJM and the PJM markets, it 
 
43 Surprisingly, this includes longstanding opponents of giving the PJM Board control over the Planning 
Protocols, such as AMP. See Lieberman, Tr. 201:23–202:3 (agreeing with Commissioner LaCerte that 
“the sous chefs should [not] have two-third voting rights authority over the chef”).  
44 Finkel Pre-Technical Conference Statement at 7. Others agreed with some or all of this idea. See Silver-
man, Tr. at 190:3–9 (§205 rights for states provides enforcement mechanism); Quinn, Tr. at 176:23–177:3 
(New England states have a “very central role” and that is a “very positive dynamic”).  
45 See Kelliher, Joseph, States cannot be granted filing rights under Section 205 of the Federal Power Act, 
UTILITY DIVE (Jul. 27, 2026), available at https://www.utilitydive.com/news/states-ferc-filing-rights-sec-
tion-205-pjm/826170/ (arguing that even granting the states the ability to force PJM to exercise its own 
filing rights under § 205—including forcing it to file a state proposal alongside its own—violates the 
law).  
46 PPL Electric Pre-Technical Conference Comments at 5, 9; Atl. City Elec. Co. v. FERC, 295 F.3d 1, 9–
11 (D.C. Cir. 2002), enforced, 329 F.3d 856 (D.C. Cir. 2003).

10 
 
makes sense to think about ways that they can retain input and potentially a check over PJM’s 
use of that power.47 This would be legally distinct from section 205 filing rights over the existing 
Tariff, which PJM holds through legal delegation from the owners of FERC-regulated assets and 
which can only be exercised by a public utility. In practice, though, it may look similar.  
 
PPL Electric offers a few additional considerations in this discussion:  
• 
The states, acting through OPSI, a governor’s collaborative, or any other group, 
already exercise significant influence at FERC. They are already able to comment 
on any PJM filing (or any other filing) and make clear their own interests and 
opinions. If they are persuasive, they can stop a PJM proposal they object to from 
moving forward. The states also have section 206 authority, including to propose 
an alternative to PJM’s proposal.  
• 
“Jump ball” filings are legally uncertain, change the nature of section 205 filings, 
and at best empower the Commission and its staff rather than their holders. The 
law on “jump ball” filings is, at best, undeveloped. While they have worked in 
other regions in extremely limited circumstances, as envisioned here, they are a 
recipe for litigation. PJM’s filings, especially in key areas like the capacity mar-
ket, move tens of billions of dollars. If the Commission is awarded the ability to 
“select” which section 205 filing it (the Commission) prefers, the proponents of 
the losing proposal have every incentive to object, forcing the region to wait for 
months or years as the process flows through the courts. This is not a recipe for 
market stability or investment. It also turns the Commission from a regulatory 
body deciding section 205 filings pursuant to law, to the decider of which 
 
47 See PPL Electric Pre-Technical Conference Comments at 12, 15.

11 
 
preferred alternative should move forward even when no section 206 complaint 
has been made.  
• 
To be successful, “matters of shared responsibility” will have to be fleshed out a 
great deal more. Mr. Finkel’s proposal was limited to “matters of shared responsi-
bility” between the states and PJM. This is clearly the right place to focus, but for 
the states to legally have a degree of control over PJM, they must delegate their 
own powers and agree to an arrangement in contract and state law, not merely 
seize the section 205 powers of FERC-regulated utilities.48  
D. 
Public Interest 
 
Finally, PPL Electric offers comment on proposals to incorporate a “public interest” 
standard into PJM’s governing documents or mission statement.49 Although that concept may ap-
pear straightforward at a high level, it raises significant questions unless carefully tied to PJM’s 
existing statutory obligations, governing documents, and Commission-approved responsibili-
ties.50 
 
Standing alone, a “public interest” mandate is vague and potentially difficult to adminis-
ter. It could mean anything that a particular advocate believes to be of value to its interests or its 
own view of the public’s needs. This inherently subjective standard risks unnecessarily 
 
48 See Mills, Tr. 120:5–8 (“it would be inconsistent from this independent discussion that we’re having for 
the states to have a jump ball right on rights that the PJM board doesn’t even have”); Finkel, Tr. 121:5–10 
(agreeing filing rights would be limited to resource adequacy and “not dealing with things the board 
doesn’t have today”).  
49 See Bowring, Tr. at 253:13–16 (“The staff should be charged with acting in the public interest”); Bruce, 
Tr. at 251:24–252:6 (introducing the concept of amending the Operating Agreement to include a public 
interest mandate).  
50 As some proponents did better than others. See Wood, Tr. at 136:10–14 (calling for “board members 
[to] have a responsibility to the public interest consistent with the FPA, which draws in the just and rea-
sonable rate”) (emphasis added).

12 
 
confusing PJM’s mission. PJM is a public utility—by some measures the largest and most im-
portant in the world—it is not a government actor. PJM is charged by existing statutory language 
and a member charter to operate the bulk electric system reliably and to administer efficient 
competitive wholesale energy markets at just and reasonable rates. It is also regulated by the 
Commission, which has its own legal standards to apply, and which is the proper democratically 
accountable actor. No matter how potentially beneficial, FERC cannot simply instruct PJM to 
adopt a different mandate not found in statute or the governing documents.51  
 
Second, because PJM is a stakeholder-driven organization, and many of those stakehold-
ers are themselves government organizations (PJM governors, OPSI and public utility commis-
sions, legislators, consumer advocates, municipalities, environmental protection organizations, 
etc.) with their own public interest mandates, adding “public interest” to PJM’s mandate intro-
duces the potential for deep conflict. If the PJM Board is supposed to act in the public interest, 
but in its independent judgment decides that standard calls for a different action than a gover-
nor’s representative or consumer advocate urges (when they are also acting in the public inter-
est), how should it resolve the matter? What if there is a conflict between the “public interest” 
and reliability? Or with just and reasonable rates? Introducing new legal concepts to complex le-
gal entities like PJM, even seemingly benign ones, is problematic and should be avoided.  
 
Third, “public interest” has a specific meaning in the context of the FPA incompatible 
with imposing a public interest mandate on PJM. It is part and parcel of the Mobile-Sierra doc-
trine by which FPA contracts may not be disturbed by FERC unless those contracts are found 
contrary to the public interest. This has been interpreted by the court to mean not anti-
 
51 See NAACP v. FPC, 425 U.S. 662 (1976) (FERC has no mandate to pursue goals beyond the FPA, even 
if they are generally accepted by society as worthy).

13 
 
competitive or fraudulent.52 A mandate that PJM not act anti-competitively or fraudulently 
leaves open a wide swath of conduct and does nothing to guide PJM in discharging its responsi-
bilities, unlike its more specific mandates to promote reliability and competition. 
 
III. 
RESPONSES TO COMMISSION QUESTIONS 
 
PPL Electric responds below to the Commission’s specific questions in the Notice Re-
questing Post-Conference Comment:53  
PJM Board Independence 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes 
No 
1) 
Should Board members’ terms be extended to five or more years? 
X 
 
 
Comments:  Longer terms would promote continuity, independence, and accountability 
by allowing Board members sufficient time to develop institutional knowledge and 
oversee longer-term market and reliability reforms. 
2) 
Should there be a maximum number of years that a Board member 
may serve (e.g., 10 years)? 
 
X 
 
Comments: The expectation may be that a Board member only serves two five-year 
terms, but in some cases it may be appropriate for someone to serve longer and the 
Commission should not set a blanket rule preventing this.  
3) 
Should the Board member qualification rules be revised to provide a 
preference for some Board members that reside in the PJM region? 
X 
 
 
Comments: PPL supports a qualified preference for geographic proximity, but not at the 
cost of candidate quality given the difficulties in finding candidates even under the cur-
rent rules.54 It might make sense to pair the preference for residing in the PJM region 
with a shortening of the cooling off period for Board members working for a Member to 
one year.  
 
52 Morgan Stanley Capital Group Inc. v. Public Util. Dist. No. 1 of Snohomish Cty., 554 U.S. 527 (2008). 
53 Post-Conference Notice.  
54 See PPL Pre-Technical Conference Comments at 6.

14 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes 
No 
4) 
Should the conflict-of-interest rules be revised to reduce the cooling 
off period for Board members from two years to one year? 
X 
 
 
Comments: See response to #3.  
5) 
Should restrictions on Board communications be relaxed to enable 
more communication between the Board and stakeholders? 
X 
 
 
Comments: PPL Electric supports reasonable changes that permit more regular, struc-
tured communication between the Board and stakeholders, provided those changes pre-
serve Board independence, confidentiality where appropriate, and the Board’s ability to 
deliberate candidly. 
6) 
In order to increase transparency, should Board votes be made public 
or the Board be required to explain its reasoning?  
 
X 
 
Comments: The PJM Board is not a regulator or government body. It needs to retain the 
ability to hold private, candid discussions related to the matters under its control and this 
requires a level of discretion that is difficult to maintain in fully public deliberations.. 
Requiring disclosure of individual Board deliberations or votes would represent a signif-
icant departure from the manner in which public utility boards generally conduct their 
business and exercise independent judgment..  
In practice, the PJM Board regularly issues public letters explaining its decisions on 
contentious items. This provides more than enough transparency without disclosing in-
dividual votes.  
7) 
In order to increase transparency, should some Board meetings be open 
or available to the public? 
 
X 
 
Comments: See response to #6. Opening Board meetings to the public would be coun-
terproductive.  
8) 
Should PJM’s governing documents be revised to explicitly state that 
the responsibility of PJM and its Board is to serve the public interest? 
 
X 
 
Comments: See detailed discussion in comments above. PJM is not a public body, and it 
would be improper to give it a public interest mandate that would conflict with its man-
date under the Federal Power Act. It would also introduce the likelihood of conflict with 
members who also have public interest mandates, but who may disagree on certain PJM 
decisions.  
9) 
Should state representatives have at least one voting member on the 
Nominating Committee? 
 
X

15 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes 
No 
 
Comments: See detailed discussion in comments above. Numerous state representatives, 
such as consumer advocates and municipalities, are PJM Members and already have rep-
resentation on the PJM Nominating Committee. Proposals to add representation from 
other state representatives, such as public utility commissioners, governors, and/or state 
legislators are at best incomplete and premature, as none of these institutions are well-
defined in the PJM governing documents and it would be irresponsible to hand over a 
role in selecting the PJM Board without much more information. Adding anything more 
than one voting member also misunderstands the function of the Nominating Commit-
tee, which seeks to operate by consensus and should not be subject to packing.  
That said, PPL Electric supports additional coordination between PJM and the states. A 
single non-voting state representative on the Nominating Committee may be an appro-
priate compromise and avenue for this coordination.  
10) 
Should PJM adopt public performance metrics and tie management 
compensation to their achievement? 
X 
 
 
Comments:  Public performance metrics may improve accountability and transparency.  
The design of any compensation framework, however, should remain within the Board’s 
discretion and support PJM’s operational and market responsibilities. 
 
Section 205 Filing Rights 
 
11) 
Should the stakeholder process be advisory, i.e., stakeholder votes only 
inform the Board? 
X 
 
 
Comments: See detailed discussion above.  
12) 
Should PJM have section 205 filing rights over the energy market and an-
cillary services unencumbered by the requirement to obtain approval of 
two-thirds of the Members Committee? 
X 
 
 
Comments: See detailed discussion above. 
13) 
Should PJM have section 205 filing rights over Regional Transmission 
Expansion Planning (RTEP) unencumbered by the requirement to obtain 
approval of two-thirds of the Members Committee? 
X 
 
 
Comments: See detailed discussion above.

16 
 
14) 
Should the Organization of PJM States Inc (OPSI) have “jump ball” rights 
over resource adequacy and transmission cost allocation filings when a 
supermajority of OPSI agrees on an alternative proposal? 
 
X 
 
Comments: OPSI is not a public utility and cannot hold section 205 rights under the 
Federal Power Act. Any formalized role for OPSI that affects PJM filings or tariff ad-
ministration would need to be carefully addressed in PJM’s governing documents and 
reviewed for consistency with the Federal Power Act, Commission precedent, and the 
limits on who may exercise public utility filing rights.  
15) 
Should the Members Committee have “jump ball” filing rights over the 
portions of the tariff where PJM has 205 filing rights when a supermajor-
ity of stakeholders approves an alternative proposal? 
 
X 
 
Comments: The PJM Members Committee is not a public utility and cannot hold sec-
tion 205 rights under the Federal Power Act. The language in the PJM Operating Agree-
ment purporting to require stakeholder approval for changes to the substantive sched-
ules was a mistake and should be corrected.55 
Stakeholder Process 
 
16) 
Should the approval threshold in the Members Committee be lowered from 
two-thirds sector-weighted voting? 
 
X 
 
Comments: The stakeholder votes should be advisory. Once this change is made, the 
thresholds for voting become irrelevant as the PJM Board will control the RTO.  
17) 
Should the voting rules barring affiliate votes, which apply to senior stand-
ing committees, also apply to lower-level committees? 
X 
 
 
Comments: Both sets of stakeholder voting rules (affiliate voting in the lower commit-
tees and sector weighted voting in the senior committees) are arbitrary. PPL agrees with 
Mr. Quinn of Vistra that the voting processes can be conformed to achieve a more effi-
cient process.56 The real solution, again, is to make the stakeholder process advisory, 
which reduces the significance of voting rules entirely.  
 
State Participation 
 
 
55 See PPL Electric Pre-Technical Conference Comments at 16.  
56 Quinn, Tr. at 156:24–158:12.

17 
 
18) 
In addition to OPSI, should there be a second state representative group 
consisting of governors’ representatives and/or state legislators’ represent-
atives? 
 
X 
 
Comments: Creating an organization for governors’ representatives and/or state legisla-
tors’ representatives does not need FERC or PJM Member permission. The states are 
free to organize themselves in any way that makes sense for them. However, as Mr. 
Mills pointed out in the technical conference, “one organization would be ideal[] for 
PJM to deal with.”57 Also, the Commission should be cautious about funding more or-
ganizations with ratepayer money in an era of affordability concerns, noting that OPSI 
and CAPS are already funded.  
19) 
Should state representatives have a formal voting role in the stakeholder 
process (limited to certain topics, such as resource adequacy and regional 
transmission cost allocation) in addition to the consumer advocate votes?  
 
X 
 
Comments: The states are not PJM Members and should not have a voting role in the 
stakeholder process (unless they become Members, similar to their role in SPP). That 
said, PPL Electric has consistently called for more state coordination with PJM—as 
sovereigns, regulators, generation planners, etc.58 Rather than engage in fights over vot-
ing power, the states should focus on these areas within their jurisdiction.  
20) 
Should PJM be required to consult with OPSI prior to making a section 
205 filing related to resource adequacy and transmission cost allocation? 
 
X 
 
Comments: PJM already regularly consults with OPSI, and PPL Electric supports con-
tinued coordination with the states.  However, converting consultation into a mandatory 
prerequisite to a section 205 filing could slow PJM’s ability to act, create procedural 
disputes unrelated to the merits of the filing, and constrain PJM’s ability to exercise its 
independent judgment.  In addition, to the extent PJM does not have the relevant section 
205 filing rights for certain transmission cost allocation matters, a mandatory OPSI con-
sultation requirement would not provide a meaningful legal mechanism for influencing 
those filings.  
 
 
57 Mills, Tr. at 92:6–23.  
58 See PPL Electric Pre-Technical Conference Comments at 8–10.

18 
 
IV. 
CONCLUSION 
 
PPL Electric thanks the Commission for raising these important topics and asks that its 
comments be considered part of the record.
